title: Rows Times Squares
context: Grade 5, the pages on the area of a rectangle and a square and Exercise 8.2. An adult sees two formulas. What the pages are doing is shortening a count: rows of squares times the squares in a row give the count, so the area of a rectangle is length x breadth, with the longer side as the length, and a square's is side x side.

writeup.why: See that rows times the squares in a row give the count, so the area of a rectangle is length x breadth and a square's is side x side, and find a breadth from a clue before multiplying.
writeup.look: A rectangle on squared paper with one row laid, the Rows handle up its breadth and the record card at the right; the Square switch on the third phase and the length strip with the Split button on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rows Times Squares' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of squares laid. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The rectangle lies on squared paper at x 120, y 250, drawn to one scale inside a box 620 by 400, its length along the bottom and labelled deep blue. The first row of violet squares, labelled Row, lies along the length. The Rows handle is a round grip at the rectangle's right edge that the child drags upward; each row it stacks lights amber for a moment. The record card stands at x 800, y 230, 300 by 260, with the columns Along the length, Along the breadth, Product and Count. The Units switch and the Square switch sit at x 800, y 520 and x 800, y 580. On the fourth phase the length strip lies at x 120, y 220, and the Split button at x 800, y 640 cuts it into three equal parts with two thin ink lines; one part drops down to stand as the breadth. The area reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with sq. cm and sq. m keys. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last rectangle stays filled with its rows, the record card beside it, and the area in green with its square unit.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the split part drops down beside the rectangle, the other two parts give a small nod, as if to say they are the same size.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet stacked. On the first phase a rectangle lies on squared paper with one row laid along its length and the Rows handle at its side. On the second a garden lies with its sides in metres and the Units switch set. On the third a board lies with the Square switch beside it. On the fourth a length strip lies above an empty rectangle, with a clue card and the Split button. One thing moves, once: the Rows handle, the Square switch or the Split button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any rectangle, stacked row by row, turned into a square, or given a breadth by the Split button. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rows times squares, length x breadth, side x side and a breadth from a clue.

source_tool.description: A rectangle is drawn on squared paper, its length along the bottom and labelled deep blue, with one row of violet squares, labelled Row, laid along it. The child drags a Rows handle up the breadth, and each row stacked lights amber for a moment and adds one row's worth to the running count. A record card at the right of the working area has four columns, Along the length, Along the breadth, Product and Count, and fills as the child works. A Units switch gives the sides centimetres or metres, and the product is then written as length x breadth with a square unit. A Square switch pulls the breadth up until it equals the length, and the line becomes side x side. On the last phase the length is also drawn as a strip, and a Split button cuts the strip into three equal parts; one part drops down beside the rectangle to become the breadth. A number pad types a count or an area with sq. cm and sq. m keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of squares laid.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count the rows again. How many squares are in each row?
voice.onNext: A new rectangle. Find the length first.
voice.opening: A rectangle, and one row of squares along it.
voice.onFinish: You turned counting squares into length times breadth.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Stack rows on any rectangle you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

phase_map.concept: Rows times squares in a row

placement.where: After the class has counted the squares of a tiled floor or a rectangle on squared paper one by one, and then counted its rows. The tool is what stacks the rows one at a time beside the count, which the printed grid shows only finished.

answer_key.rule: Squares along the length x squares along the breadth gives the count, the same as counting one by one. So the area of a rectangle is length x breadth, with the longer side as the length; lengths in cm give sq. cm and lengths in m give sq. m. A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are equal, so its area is side x side. A breadth given as one third of the length is found first: one third of a length is the length split into three equal parts. Then multiply. The screen in the opening box has rough measures, so any area worked from them is an estimate, said with about.
answer_key.wrong: The rows the child stacked stay, and the stage counts them again one row at a time beside the child's number, lighting amber the row or the side that differs. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Each row along the length has 9 squares.
There are 5 rows, one for each square along the breadth.
9 x 5 = 45, the same as counting every square one by one.
items.question: A rectangle on squared paper has 9 squares along its length and 5 along its breadth. How many squares does it cover?
items.checkpoint: Rows times the squares in a row gives the count.
items.misconception: Adding the squares along the length and the breadth, which counts one row and one column, not the whole surface.

steps: The longer side, 16 m, is the length, and 7 m is the breadth.
The area of a rectangle is length x breadth: 16 x 7 = 112.
So the area of a 16 m by 7 m rectangle is 112 sq. m.
items.question: A garden is 16 m long and 7 m wide. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: Lengths in m give an area in sq. m.
items.misconception: Adding the length and the breadth, which gives a length in metres, not a surface.

steps: A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are equal.
So its area is side x side: 15 x 15 = 225.
So the area of a square of side 15 cm is 225 sq. cm.
items.question: A square board has sides of 15 cm. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: A square's area is side x side.
items.misconception: Taking four lots of the side, which gives the perimeter, a length, not the area.

steps: One third of 27 cm is 9 cm, because 3 x 9 = 27.
The area of a rectangle 27 cm long and 9 cm wide is 27 x 9 = 243 sq. cm.
items.question: A rectangle is 27 cm long, and its breadth is one third of its length. What is its area?
items.checkpoint: Find the breadth from the clue first, then multiply.
items.misconception: Multiplying the length by three to find the breadth, which makes the breadth longer than the length.

teaching_notes: Count one rectangle square by square, then count its rows and the squares in a row, before the tool opens. Name the longer side the length before multiplying, so the words match the picture. A square is a rectangle whose length and breadth are equal. Say one third of the length, and find the breadth before multiplying. The screen question in the opening box can be tried now and stays the child's; its measures are rough, so any answer is an estimate, said with about. The printed rectangles and squares are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a rows times squares tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A rectangle is drawn on squared paper with its length along the bottom, labelled deep blue, and one row of violet squares, labelled Row, laid along it. A Rows handle dragged up the breadth stacks one row at a time, each lighting amber briefly and adding a row's worth to the count.
